Name: David Moe
Question: Why do so many Canadians sound almost Irish but not British?
Answer: I knew an Irish woman who moved from Ireland to Newfoundland to work as a doctor. She couldn’t understand a single word her first patient said. No, it is not the same accent. The Newfoundland accent is an archaic dialect closer to Elizabethan and Shakespearian English than modern English or Irish. Modern English has drifted from its origins so the English no longer pronounce their “r”s. On the other hand, the accent in Nova Scotia (which means New Scotland), is closer to Scottish. There is a strong Scottish influence on Canadian English. The Montreal English accent has strong French influence, although it is peasant French as someone from Paris once told me. He couldn’t even understand their French so he had to speak English. From Toronto on West, the country was settled so fast it didn’t have time to develop an accent of its own, so Toronto and Vancouver English is very similar to Southern California English. I grew up in Central Alberta, and I loved the movie “Fargo” because the actors sounded just like my relatives who lived in Fargo, North Dakota. I can hear the sing-song intonation and odd words they brought over from the Scandinavian countries. Although third generation Canadian, I can speak a little Norwegian myself. However, the school systems Canadianize immigrant children so while they may all look different, they all sound the same — more similar to the standard American accent than most Americans speak.

Name: David Moe
Question: Why do so many Europeans think they can do a cross country trip of Canada in a couple weeks/a month? Is it just because they don't understand how big a country Canada is and that we don't have the level of high speed train service they do?
Answer: I think the problem is that they have never experienced such a big country. Canada is bigger than the EU, but with 1/12 of the population. Driving from Victoria BC to St. John’s Newfoundland is like driving from Lisbon Portugal to Moscow Russsia — not something you want do in a week — and when you do, you are going to see a lot of unpopulated forest with nothing but rocks and trees and water, and a lot of prairie farmland with hardly any people. The average Canadian province is bigger than any country in Europe except Russia, and we have parks bigger than Switzerland. You can tell them that, but they can’t imagine it. They have to experience it to believe it. As for high speed train service, Canada’s much lower population density makes it uneconomic and the cities are too far apart. Flying by jet airliner is much more practical. I used to annoy Brits by telling them that if London and Paris were in Canada, they would be in the same province — Calgary and Edmonton are the same distance apart while Toronto and Montreal are twice as far apart. Those are the only two Canadian city pairs for which high speed rail would be practical.

Name: David Moe
Question: I brush and floss my teeth everyday but still get cavities. I noticed people in third world countries get less cavities, why is that? Does their food contain probotic cultures?
Answer: Prior to the invention of agriculture, almost nobody got cavities because they got very little carbohydrates and sugar in their diets. After agriculture was introduced, the carbohydrates in grain caused cavities in people’s teeth. Archeologists can date the arrival of agriculture in various regions by looking at the teeth on old skeletons to see if they had cavities. After sugar started being produced in industrial quantities, the number of cavities increased. Studies of old skeleteons show that on British naval ships, the officers had far more cavities than the common sailors because they could afford sugar in their food. People in third world countries may have fewer cavities because they don’t get much sugar in their food. The bacteria in your mouth that thrive on carbohydrates and sugars generate acid that eats through the enamel on your teeth. Your first line of defense against that, other than cutting down on carbohydrates and eliminating sugar, is to have fluoride in your water, which will strengthen your tooth enamel by changing its chemical constitution. Your second line of defense is your dentist, who will recommend a fluoride toothpaste.

Name: David Moe
Question: Canada has abolished the cent. Don't you think it should abolish prices ending in cents? It is never to my advantage, hence how many millions go to the government that has its hand in my pockets?
Answer: Canada has not abolished the cent, it has just stopped minting 1 cent coins because it costs 2 cents to mint a penny. Hardly anybody uses actual physical money any more. It is almost all electronic transfers, where they round to the nearest cent. In cash transactions they round to the nearest 5 cents and it averages out the same. I used to get into arguments with accountants about rounding errors because they thought all numbers were exact, and I had to point out that there were always rounding errors in them. In IT, we used bankers rounding for them because it was standard, not exact. I took a lot more mathematics in university than they did, and could tell them exactly how inexact their numbers were. I remember one time on lunch break at work I was booking a mountain ski chalet for a week for 20 people when the batteries in my cell phone died. I picked up my office phone and called to complete the transaction, which was for thousands of dollars. A few weeks later, the head of Telecommunications called me into her office and informed me I had made an unauthorized telephone call on a company phone. I said, well, OK, how much did it cost? She said 63 cents. I pulled 65 cents in coins out of my pocket and put it on her desk. She just picked it up without saying thank you. I said, “Where are my 2 cents change”. She just glared at me because she thought I was being sarcastic, which of course I was. What is she going to do, fire me? According to HR, it would cost the company $100,000 to replace me. And then I would be working for their competition, knowing all their secrets. And why was she quibbling over 63 cents when the company was losing millions? The old British phrase for people like this is “Penny wise, pound foolish”.

Name: David Moe
Question: Why haven’t I met my boyfriend’s family? We have been bf/gf for 3 months but we’ve known each other for 9. He has never refused but hasn't brought it up at all. Should I be concerned?
Answer: Meeting the family can be kind of a momentous occasion. It is the time where they scrutinize you closely and decide whether you are acceptable marriage material or not. You need to approach it with some trepidation, which is what he is doing. I can remember when my little sister (who was 30 years old by then) brought her boyfriend home to meet the family. I aske her, “Well, it is serious then, isn’t it?”. She said no, she just thought he should meet the family. I said, “Don’t lie to me little sister. When was the last time you brought a boyfriend home? Never, right? You didn’t bring the Venezuelan millionaire or the air force pilot home, but you did bring this guy home. Don’t tell me it’s not serious.” I could hear wedding bells chiming in the distance. Our mother didn’t like him but she only got one vote and my sister was determined. I can also remember when my brother brought his girl friend home to meet the family. She was a quiet shy girl and sat in the kitchen while we were talking in the living room. Our mother had to coax her out and tell her, “Come into the living room with the family, we won’t bite you.” Later my brother-in-law bet my brother $20 that he would marry her. My brother took that bet, and eventually lost $20. Do you think the family can’t read the signs? We have extra-sensory perception.
